items.title: Bobby Watson interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, January 19, 1996
items.q: as much as I try to sound like Cannonball and Bird, I sound like Bob.

ctx.x: Oh, that’s wonderful. Tell us, get us inside of one of your original compositions. What goes through your mind when you write a tune and what parameters do you exploit to try to capture the voice of Bobby Watson in a jazz composition?

Well capturing my voice is really not too hard, because as I discovered on the saxophone, as much as I try to sound like Cannonball and Bird, I sound like Bob. So the thing is to accept who you are. That’s the hardest thing. And once you accept who you are, then it’s really easy because I work with Sam Rivers, and he’s avante garde. And he’s in his 60s

but as he reminds me, when he played bebop, that was avante garde. So he’s always been avante garde. And we were on a train one time over in Europe and we were with this group of tenor saxophones called the Winds of Manhattan. And he said let me show you something. Because I was watching and he’d be writing without no piano. And sometimes he’d cut this page and put it over here, and he’d just be writing, without a score. And he says, I said, “How do you do that?” And he says, “Here, take a bit of paper. Write…
